sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: On the night of the Eaton Fire in January 2025, Anthony Mitchell, 68, was at home in west Altadena with his son Justin, 35. Anthony used a wheelchair. Justin has cerebral palsy. Anthony called 911 at 6:03am and again at 6:14. The dispatcher told him "They're on their way." Nobody came. Both men died in their home. LA County's paratransit service later said its vans were ready by 4am. Nobody called it. The vehicles existed. What failed was coordination. A UN survey of about 6,000 people with disabilities found that only 1 in 5 could evacuate right away without difficulty. During Hurricane Harvey, fewer than 5% of the people on Texas's disability registry were contacted, because nobody had the staff to call through the list in time. We took that problem to Palo Alto Fire Stations 1 and 6. "We have four dispatchers that sit in the room," one firefighter told us. "You can only answer so many calls." Standard Response is our answer.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Standard Response is an evacuation coordination system: it calls every home in a warning zone, triages who can't get out, routes accessible vehicles and neighbors to them, and keeps every promise to a resident true while the plan changes. A simulated night over the real map of west Altadena. Standard Response has called every home inside the warning zone (white outline) while the fire (top right) moves in. The 1,003 red homes are the ones dispatch has to reach. Ready check: Before any disaster, the agent calls each household (or they sign up at /ready ) and records who needs help and which room they sleep in. A household that would need a ride is paired with the nearest neighbor within 900 m who said they'd drive. Warning calls: A dispatcher draws the zone on the rescue map, or our public Apify Actor starts the calls when a California county issues a warning. The agent calls every home at once and reads each answer back for correction. Life threats jump to the top of the call floor. Neighbors: On every call, the agent asks whether anyone else on the street might not be able to leave, and matches the names people give to homes on file. It calls a resident's named helper first. If nobody is named, it calls the nearest neighbor with a car and says what the pickup takes before they agree. sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Twilio carries every call, Cartesia hears and speaks it, Claude reads each turn and Moss supplies the agency's approved answers. One Convex database connects everything, so no service calls another directly. Each sponsor's part is described below. Dispatch and simulation: Our adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) runs over an OSMnx road graph of Altadena, with OR-Tools and a greedy heuristic as baselines. The night simulator runs on SimPy. The voice server runs on Fly.io and the dispatch solver on DigitalOcean. The dispatch math Every request has a deadline 10 minutes before fire is expected at the home. A rider who boards by the deadline counts zero expected deaths. After the deadline, the count climbs linearly to the household's full risk 600 seconds later. The optimizer minimizes sum over requests (10^7 x expected deaths + need weight x arrival time) + sum over vehicles (driving time) subject to each vehicle's seats, wheelchair spaces and stretcher spaces. One expected death outweighs any amount of driving, and the need-weighted waiting term spreads riders across the fleet. The search ( dispatch/alns.py ) tears plans apart and rebuilds them under simulated annealing. It never moves a run a driver has accepted. On our fastest simulated fire it completes a median of 6 more on-time pickups than the greedy heuristic over 100 seeds.

devpost_page.tagline: Learn and build infrastructures in hours, not weeks

sections.text: Infraflow

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Developing and managing cloud infrastructure can be intimidating for beginners, especially students who rarely have hands-on access to DevOps technology. The steep learning curve often discourages newcomers from exploring the possibilities of infrastructure as code. Infraflow was inspired by the need for a user-friendly, approachable way to experience DevOps concepts without being overwhelmed. By enabling users to turn diagrams into Terraform code, Infraflow makes cloud infrastructure accessible, helping bridge the gap between visual understanding and real-world implementation.

sections.heading: What it Does
sections.text: Infraflow provides a simple way for users to design cloud infrastructure visually and instantly generate the corresponding Terraform code. Users can create diagrams of their desired infrastructure setup, select resources, and connect them visually. Infraflow then translates this visual layout into clean, readable Terraform code that users can deploy directly. This allows students and beginners to learn about DevOps, Terraform, and cloud infrastructure by experimenting in a user-friendly, interactive environment.

sections.heading: How We Built It
sections.text: Infraflow was built using: Frontend : A diagramming interface for creating and connecting cloud resources, using [library/tool name, e.g., React with a diagramming library like D3.js or JointJS]. Backend : A server that processes the visual diagrams, translates them into Terraform code, and provides this code to the user. Terraform : Infraflow generates Terraform configuration files for various providers, allowing the generated code to be deployed to cloud platforms like AWS, Azure, or GCP. Bun and Express : We used Bun for efficient TypeScript handling and an Express server for handling user requests and generating Terraform files based on the diagram inputs.

sections.heading: Challenges We Ran Into
sections.text: Diagram-to-Code Translation : Mapping diagram elements accurately to Terraform resources required us to establish a clear, flexible schema for translating visual components to code. User Experience : We aimed to keep the interface simple yet effective for students with little or no experience in DevOps, which led to several design iterations. Handling Multiple Providers : Infraflow needed to support different cloud providers, each with unique Terraform syntax and configurations, making it challenging to create a consistent user experience across platforms.

sections.heading: Accomplishments That We're Proud Of
sections.text: User-Friendly Interface : We developed an intuitive interface that makes creating infrastructure diagrams easy and fun for beginners. Instant Terraform Code Generation : Infraflow successfully translates diagrams into functional Terraform code in real time, making DevOps accessible and tangible. Cross-Provider Support : We implemented multi-cloud support, allowing users to explore infrastructure setups across different providers without needing to learn new tools.

sections.heading: What We Learned
sections.text: This project helped us dive deep into DevOps principles, infrastructure as code, and the challenges of making complex concepts beginner-friendly. We gained hands-on experience with Terraform, Bun, TypeScript, and diagramming libraries, enhancing our skills in both frontend design and backend logic.

sections.heading: What's Next for Infraflow
sections.text: Enhanced Customization : Adding more options for customizing resource properties within the diagrams. Deployment from Infraflow : Allowing users to deploy directly from the Infraflow interface to their cloud provider, streamlining the learning process further. Educational Resources : Providing guided lessons on cloud infrastructure and DevOps directly within the platform. Advanced Integrations : Expanding support for more providers, infrastructure configurations, and more complex setups, such as Kubernetes clusters or CI/CD pipelines.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: One of our teammates has a friend who runs a flea-market stall selling apparel. From hearing about their experience, we saw how much work goes into running a small pop-up business: keeping track of products and stock, recording payments, understanding expenses, and figuring out how much the event actually earned. These tasks often live in different places, which makes it difficult to get a clear picture during or after an event. A vendor might know that some items sold, but still have to reconcile sales, remaining inventory, transaction activity, and event fees before deciding what to bring next time. That conversation inspired us to build Bazaarly: a tool that connects event inventory and checkout with financial tracking and sales analysis. We want vendors to spend less time piecing together records and more time understanding how their business is performing.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Bazaarly is a React and TypeScript dashboard for pop-up apparel events. Vendors can organize garment inventory by event, review product details and stock statuses, and see sales activity associated with each event. The checkout prototype uses Solana Pay on Devnet. A customer can initiate a payment for an item, and Bazaarly records the sale only after the payment is confirmed on the Solana network. Event sales records and summaries use the item’s USD price, so vendors can review results in familiar dollar values. This is a Devnet prototype; it does not process real-money payments. For each event, Bazaarly summarizes confirmed revenue and sales activity, with product and category breakdowns. It also tracks vendor-fee coverage and provides a sales ledger for reviewing recorded transactions. Vendors can compare completed events to understand how their results differ and use that information when planning future inventory. We also explored using the Nessie sandbox banking API for a financial-management dashboard. The prototype is intended to help vendors review simulated account and customer activity, track money coming in and going out, and get a clearer view of cash flow. Nessie provides simulated banking data, so this part demonstrates the dashboard concept rather than connecting to a vendor’s real bank account. In addition, we developed a separate Snowflake Cortex sales-consultant prototype. It accepts uploaded sales CSV files, calculates metrics such as total revenue, average

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: The main Bazaarly dashboard uses React and TypeScript for the user interface, with Firebase and Firestore for application data. Events and inventory are organized so vendors can review products and sales in the context of a specific event. The Solana Pay checkout runs as a separate app and connects to Bazaarly through the checkout flow. We treat a sale as complete only after the Devnet transaction is confirmed; creating a payment request alone does not add a confirmed sale to event analytics. The Nessie prototype uses simulated banking data to demonstrate cash-flow and customer/account activity views. The Snowflake Cortex consultant uses a Node.js backend: it processes uploaded sales CSV data and calculates metrics on the server before sending the structured figures to the model.

sections.heading: Challenges and lessons
sections.text: A key challenge was deciding when a sale should count as a sale. A checkout request and a confirmed on-chain payment are different events. We designed the prototype so event reporting relies on confirmed payments, helping keep the sales ledger and analytics tied to completed transactions. We also learned that QR payment compatibility can vary between wallets and devices. A payment flow that works in one wallet may behave differently in another, so wallet interoperability needs testing as part of the checkout experience. Another challenge was bringing financial activity and sales analysis into a useful view without overstating what the prototypes can do. Nessie’s simulated account data can demonstrate how a cash-flow dashboard might work, while Snowflake Cortex can analyze metrics from an uploaded sales file. Neither prototype currently reads live financial or sales data from the main Bazaarly app.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.text: Our first priority is letting vendors record what they paid for each item when it’s added to inventory, so Bazaarly can show true profit and margin by item, category and event instead of just revenue. We also want to test with real vendors to see whether the insights change how they stock and price. Nessie is a sandbox, so a production version would need a real financial-data provider and a secure connection to vendors’ accounts.

devpost_page.tagline: Perception layer for robotic pollinators. Analyzes bee-to-flower visits while simulating robotic pollinators that learn efficient routes from real bee behavior.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Pollinators are disappearing, and about a third of the food we grow depends on them. We wanted to turn camera footage into something actionable: which flowers got visited, which didn't, and how a pollinator robot could achieve perception.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Pollensight turns ordinary fixed-camera video into a per-flower record of insect visits. It can aslo forecast where an insect will go next and plans a robot route to the flowers it missed. Video : tracks insects with boxes and trails. Flower boxes light up during a visit, and a timeline shows every visit. Search : plain-English natural-language search across clips ( "when does the bee land on a flower?" ) that jumps the video straight to that moment. Analytics : visits, dwell time, transit time, flight speed, revisits and a heatmap of where the insect spent its time. Forecast : the insect's predicted path for the next 2 seconds, shown as a spread of possible futures, plus the odds for its next flower and how much longer it will stay. Field : on farm clips, flowers are colored by how many visits they still need, with a robot route that covers the most of them within a time budget. Dataset : accuracy across all 48 clips, with the visual audits behind every number. Upload : analyze your own fixed-camera video. Simulations : a bee trained with reinforcement learning flies over a random flower field it has never seen, in interactive 3D. The same flight is rendered in MuJoCo , with a Crazyflie 2 drone standing in for the bee.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: Pollensight is a four-stage pipeline. Perception (Python, OpenCV, NumPy): OpenCV background subtraction and connected components find moving blobs, and a dynamic-programming search links them into flight paths. Every half second we send a 160 px crop to Perceptron's Mk1.5 vision model to check that there's really an insect there, and we keep a path only if at least 70% of its crops are confirmed. Mk1.5 also finds flowers in a median frame, which gives us stable flower IDs for detecting visits. Perceptron API layer: we wrote our own client on top of the perceptron SDK. It uses box, point and clip annotations, JSON-schema output and the Files API for video. Every answer is cached under a SHA-256 key, so the whole project replays offline for free . Intelligence: Forecasting (scikit-learn): a k-nearest-neighbors "path fan" for the next 2 seconds, gradient-boosted next-flower prediction and Monte Carlo rollouts. These are trained on 2,335 real insect flights and tested on camera stations the model never saw. Route planning: an orienteering planner (greedy insertion plus 2-opt) that picks the most valuable flowers to visit within a time budget. Simulation: a Gymnasium environment with a Stable-Baselines3 PPO bee, replayed in MuJoCo using the Crazyflie 2 model from MuJoCo Menagerie. Web app (React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8): Canvas 2D and SVG overlays, a three.js 3D Simulations page, and custom Vite middleware that streams video with HTTP range requests and runs the Python forecast, an

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: Result Insect tracking (48 clips) 90% of the path covered, median error ≈ 3–4 px Visit detection (farm clips) 90% of detected visits are real ( 64% without Mk1.5) Flower detection 98% precision, 87% recall Next-flower prediction (unseen cameras) right flower in the top 3 picks 79% of the time (nearest-flower guess: 68%) Robot route delivers 39–56% of missing visits in 30 s (random order: 17–33%) We also built a full pipeline that anyone can reproduce: 45 tests run offline and 144/144 data files pass validation . sections.heading: What we learned
sections.text: This project was our way into physical AI . None of us had built AI that acts in the real world before, and we learned how to do it by using computer vision to turn raw video into data that a forecaster, a route planner and a robot can act on. Pairing a cheap classical tracker with a strong vision model that checks its work beats either one alone. Mk1.5 raised visit precision from 64% to 90%.

sections.text: Tiny, fast insects on busy backgrounds. Plain motion tracking picked up leaves moving in the wind, and running a vision model on every frame was too slow and too expensive. We compared against each dataset's own reference tracker and visually audited the flower detections, rather than trusting results that just looked right. Four people editing overlapping code at the same time. Agreeing on fixed JSON formats ( CONTRACT.md ) and a validator early on kept everyone's work compatible.

devpost_page.title: Starward
devpost_page.tagline: Starward shows you exactly where on your hike your phone can text by satellite, so you know before you go dark, and someone at home knows if you don't check in.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Living in the Pacific Northwest, we're surrounded by incredible hiking trails and outdoor destinations. Washington has so many beautiful places to explore, but one common problem with hiking in remote areas is losing cell service. Whether you're hiking through the mountains or exploring a trail deep in the forest, it can be difficult to communicate with anyone if something goes wrong. We wanted to address this problem because staying connected shouldn't require buying expensive satellite equipment or worrying about whether your phone will work. With newer phones beginning to support satellite messaging, we saw an opportunity to make this technology more accessible and useful for hikers. This inspired us to create Starward, a platform that helps people prepare for hikes, understand where satellite communication might work, and keep their loved ones informed along the way.

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Starward is a hiking safety platform that helps users plan communication before heading somewhere without reliable cell service. Users start by selecting a hiking trail, date, start time, phone model, and carrier. Starward then analyzes satellite orbit data, terrain elevation, and phone compatibility to estimate where satellite messaging is most likely to work along their route. The results are displayed on an interactive, color-coded map showing areas with stronger or weaker estimated satellite connectivity. Starward also recommends check-in locations and time windows so hikers can plan where and when to contact someone. Additionally, Starward includes a wireless recommendation system that determines whether a user would benefit from an additional satellite service, such as T-Mobile's T-Satellite. Instead of encouraging unnecessary purchases, our system prioritizes the most affordable solution, even if that means recommending that the user buy nothing. Users can share their trip plan with an emergency contact through our Photon messaging integration. Hikers can then send a simple "OK" message to check in, allowing their contacts to receive updates. Starward also includes a missed-check-in alert feature to help contacts identify when someone may need assistance.

sections.heading: How we built it
sections.text: We built Starward using Python, Flask, JavaScript, HTML, and Folium to create an interactive web application. For satellite coverage estimates, we integrated real orbital data from CelesTrak, using Skyfield and SGP4 to calculate satellite positions. We combined this with trail information from OpenStreetMap and elevation data to estimate how terrain might affect satellite visibility. We then visualized this information through an interactive map that highlights different coverage conditions along the trail. We also created a recommendation engine that evaluates users' phone models, carriers, available satellite services, and pricing to identify suitable connectivity options. For communication, we integrated Photon Spectrum through a Node.js messaging bridge connected to our Flask backend. This enables the application to send trip details and check-in notifications through a messaging service. Throughout development, we used Cursor and Claude Code to help implement features, debug issues, understand unfamiliar technologies, and integrate different components. We used these tools to accelerate development while reviewing and testing our code as a team.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: One of our biggest challenges was figuring out how to combine several different technologies into one project that would actually be useful. We wanted Starward to be more than just a satellite coverage map, so we spent time thinking about what hikers would realistically need before and during a trip. Another major challenge was integrating Photon with our Flask web application. Our backend and messaging service used different technologies, so we had to build a bridge between them and work through configuration, message delivery, and communication between the services. We also faced challenges with validating satellite coverage predictions. Satellite visibility depends on several factors, including orbital positions, surrounding terrain, and environmental obstructions. We had to combine multiple data sources while recognizing that our predictions could only be estimates rather than guarantees. Finally, coordinating our different components was challenging because the mapping, recommendation, frontend, and messaging systems were developed in parallel. Making everything work together required debugging, testing, and communication across the team.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we're proud of
sections.text: One of our biggest accomplishments was integrating Photon into our web application and getting the messaging functionality connected to our hiking safety workflow. Building a system that could connect a trip plan with text-based communication was especially exciting because it made Starward feel like more than just a website. We're also proud of combining real satellite orbital data and terrain information to build an interactive hiking map. Seeing how these different datasets could work together to provide useful information was rewarding. Another accomplishment was building a recommendation engine that doesn't automatically try to sell users something. We wanted Starward to make decisions based on what would actually benefit the hiker, including telling them when their current phone and service are already sufficient. Most importantly, we're proud that we were able to bring together multiple technical components into a working local web application during a hackathon.

sections.heading: What we learned

sections.text: Homefull

sections.heading: The Inspiration
sections.text: Our team know many people who either are homeless or were homeless in the past due to past mistakes, unfair accusations or unfortunate circumstances. Being homeless is more than just a struggle for money, lack of shelter can lead to sitting in the cold getting frostbite or even hypothermia leading to more debt. Having barely any money, unable to feed yourself and difficulty in securing water. After all this hard it is to be homeless and amount of homeless people unaware of the resources available to them, we thought that it would be a good idea to make an app to help them find out.

sections.heading: Setting up
sections.text: After realizing what idea we wanted to do it was a bit of challenge understanding how we would do it. I mean we can't exactly make a web app our strong suit since most homeless people don't really have a full desktop setup, so we had to start working on a mobile app. We didn't have experience in mobile app development, but we split up our roles for two person each on frontend of the app and backend with the AI and scraping of information. It was a real struggle to even setup a map view for the app, but thanks to a library we were able to make a map with just: import React from 'react'; import MapView from 'react-native-maps'; <View style={styles.container}> <MapView style={styles.map} /> </View> we will definitely not run into problems with this library since it was made before react (foreshadowed).

sections.heading: Bumps and Bruises
sections.text: Our main challenges was just trying to adapt because we had no experience with mobile development or agentic AI, not mention the hard time debugging due to rate limiting and merge conflicts. However as I not so subtlety foreshadowed we ran into a big problem where a lot of the features of the map library we were using had been deprecated such as labels, so we had to use other methods like a search bar and menu. We had some plans to use software such as Eleven labs instead, to give an audio cue rather than nothing, however due to the amount of API calls we were already making our team decided it would be too costly in time and money for the amount of gain. In the end we were able to finish all of the front end and optimize it to only require 1 API call then an O(n) operation to sort it correctly.

sections.heading: The Backend: Cogs and Cogs and Cogs and Cogs...
sections.text: The backend of our application was hosted on a Digital Ocean cloud compute virtual machine. We were lucky enough to have $200 of credits to work with and a powerful Nvidia data center card wit 141GB of vram. Nemotron the Hedgehog For our project we decided to leverage the power of Nvidia Nemotron 70B on ollama to make good use of the computing power we have access to. The use of Nemotron as our agentic AI allows our application to perform more in depth and precise research tailored to the location and needs of the users. In the beginning we struggled to work with and design of our application using agentic AI due to the new design paradigms we had to adapt to. We ended up designing small python functions that perform specific tasks so that the AI can call them as needed. First we implemented functions that take a urls and and search for relevant information to our problem area such as finding information about when and where free meals are being given out by churches or wen and where harm reduction outreach is happening. Then, to keep leveraging the powers of agentic AI, we connected it to DuckDuck Go search API so that it can search for sites on its own and continue gathering useful information. We originally ran the AI in a docker container for a consistent development environment and portability, but we ran into issues fully utilizing the GPU. We found that CUDA pass through was becoming too much of a hassle and a time sink so we decided just run it on the machine itself s

sections.heading: Epilogue
sections.text: Although we were able to create our original vision, we were not able to implement all the ideas that we had envisioned. Some features we were excited for was highlighting areas where it was legal to pitch a tent, give adverts for areas that are at risk of flooding, and using a queue that is constantly being filled with URLs for our AI continuously find new information and resources. The good thing about some of these ideas is that all it would take was fine tuning the model and the system prompt plus some more work on the frontend. This project showed us that agentic AI shines when we expose small utility functions as tools the model can call, which makes the system more general and easier to extend. We truly see a lot of potential in this application to be helpful and useful to those in need.

sections.heading: Inspiration
sections.text: Every night, medical writers at pharma companies paste confidential clinical trial documents into ChatGPT to clean up the grammar. Pharmacovigilance specialists draft SAE narratives with patient quasi-identifiers in the prompt. Regulatory affairs teams paste FDA response letters to get help with wording. 58% of front-line health staff use unapproved AI tools for work, and 44% of them admit to including identifiable patient data at least occasionally. The current options are bad. You can block the tools entirely, and staff route around you on personal devices. You can sign a BAA with an enterprise tier, but the sanctioned tools lag in capability, so people still use shadow AI for the hard stuff. You can run regex-based DLP, but it either over-redacts and destroys clinical meaning or under-redacts and leaks. What's worse, compliance training focuses on the 18 HIPAA Safe Harbor identifiers — names, SSNs, MRNs — but the most damaging leakage in clinical trials isn't PHI at all. It's Material Non-Public Information: compound codenames that reveal a company's pipeline strategy, interim efficacy readouts that could move stock prices in the billions, amendment rationales that signal safety problems before the sponsor announces them. No regex catches "ORR of 47% in the 200mg arm versus 22% in control." That's the gap we set out to fill. We expected to build a privacy tool and show it worked. What we actually built is a privacy tool and an adversarial harness that measures where and wh

sections.heading: What it does
sections.text: Asclepius is a local privacy layer that sits between clinical trial staff and cloud LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT). It intercepts sensitive documents, processes them through a three-stage pipeline running entirely on-device, and forwards only a safe proxy to the cloud. The response comes back, original entities are re-applied locally, and the user gets a useful answer — without any PHI or proprietary IP ever leaving their machine. The pipeline has three layers: Safe Harbor Stripper — deterministic regex + local NER detection of all 18 HIPAA identifiers, replaced with tagged placeholders like <PATIENT_NAME_1> , <DATE_2> . The entity map is stored locally and never leaves the process. Neural Router — a locally-running LLM classifies each request into one of three paths: Abstract-extractable (~70% target): task intent can be expressed without any sensitive entities. The local model rewrites the query from scratch. The mapping is non-injective: multiple inputs produce the same synthesized query, making inversion mathematically impossible. DP-tolerant (~20% target): the task needs some content but not exact values. Hidden-state embeddings are clipped to bounded L2 norm and perturbed with calibrated Gaussian noise, providing formal $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy guarantees. Local-only (~10% target): content and task are inseparable. The local model answers entirely on-device, nothing is sent to the cloud. sections.text: Architecture. A modular Python pipeline with strict separation of concerns. Every module — Safe Harbor stripper, router, query synthesizer, DP mechanism, proxy decoder, remote client, answer applier — is independently testable. All model calls (local LM and remote Anthropic) go through wrappers that enforce audit logging, canary detection, and hash-only output (no raw content in logs). Synthetic corpus. 1,200 structurally realistic clinical trial documents across four types: Serious Adverse Event narratives (500), protocol excerpts (200), CRA monitoring visit reports (200), and Clinical Study Report drafts (300). Every document has ground-truth sensitive-span annotations with precise character offsets, covering 18 HIPAA categories plus clinical quasi-identifiers (compound codes, site IDs, doses, indications, efficacy values, AE grades) and MNPI categories (interim results, amendment rationales, regulatory questions). All content is visibly synthetic — investigators named "Dr. Testname Alpha," sites like "Synthetic Regional Medical Center." Attack suite. Five adversarial classes, each evaluated at every iteration of the system: A1. Verbatim scan — literal + fuzzy substring matching of ground-truth spans against proxy text A2. Cross-encoder similarity — cosine similarity of proxy and original via all-MiniLM-L6-v2 , with a 0.85 danger threshold A3. Trained span inversion — DistilBERT token classifier trained to recover sensitive spans from proxy text (our primary threat model) A

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into
sections.text: The embedding–text privacy gap. This is the headline finding, and it surfaced by accident. We swept ε across ${0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0}$ expecting to see a smooth privacy-utility curve. What we saw instead was utility of exactly 0.8598 at every ε to six decimal places . The σ values ranged from 9.69 (at ε=0.5) to 0.97 (at ε=5.0) — a 10× variation. At ε=0.5, the injected noise had L2 magnitude roughly 438× the clipped signal. And the output text was bit-identical . The diagnostic took a day to build and a minute to confirm: noise is injected correctly into the hidden state, but the proxy decoder ignores it. The decoder projects the noisy vector onto the vocabulary embedding matrix to extract top-k nearest tokens as soft hints, then passes them to a paraphrase prompt that explicitly tells the model hints can be discarded. Under greedy decoding (temperature 0) anchored to the placeholder-substituted input, the paraphrase is a deterministic function of the text — not of the hint. The $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP guarantee holds mathematically on the embedding. It does not propagate to the text surface. The decoder is ignoring the mechanism we built. This is not an implementation bug. It's a structural mismatch between where DP is defined (vector representations) and where the adversary operates (token sequences). devpost_page.title: Cognita
devpost_page.tagline: Agentic Onboarding - From Documents to Interactive Learning

sections.heading: Inspiration ✨
sections.text: Intern onboarding often feels overwhelming. New hires are handed hundreds of pages of PDFs, manuals, and policies, and are expected to absorb them quickly. We’ve gone through this ourselves and realized that traditional onboarding is both time-consuming for HR and ineffective for interns. We wanted to build a system that transforms static documentation into personalized, interactive lessons that make learning faster and more engaging.

sections.heading: What does it do? 🤔
sections.text: Cognita takes company documents and turns them into interactive learning experiences. Companies upload training materials, and interns can then ask questions about their roles or processes. Instead of a generic answer, Cognita generates a short, tailored lesson with multiple sections. Each section can include interactive components such as multiple choice questions, fill-in-the-blanks, code examples, drag-and-drop activities, or diagrams. Progress is tracked automatically so both interns and companies can see how knowledge is being absorbed.

sections.heading: How we built it 🏰
sections.text: We designed Cognita around a RAG pipeline. PyMuPDF handles PDF extraction with text chunking that preserves context. We use ChromaDB and Gemini Embeddings for embedding storage and semantic search. The AI core is powered by Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro, which generates structured JSON lessons through carefully engineered prompts. The frontend parses this JSON and renders each lesson as React components that manage state, track progress, and log interactions. Analytics are collected for each component and fed back to the system, enabling Cognita to generate targeted follow-up lessons when interns struggle with a concept.

sections.heading: Challenges we ran into 😠
sections.text: Our biggest challenge was database state management. Each lesson contains multiple interactive components, and we needed a schema that could track progress in real time, not just right or wrong answers, but attempts, time spent, and completion status, while keeping state consistent across the frontend and backend. Synchronizing these updates proved difficult, since every user interaction had to feed back into the database without losing context. On top of that, we also had to refine prompts to prevent the AI Agent from giving overly short answers, implement retry logic, and experiment with PDF chunking strategies to preserve formatting while staying within token limits.

sections.heading: Accomplishments that we’re proud of 👏
sections.text: We built a complete pipeline where documents are processed, lessons are generated, and adaptive feedback loops are maintained. The frontend renders lessons as clean, interactive modules rather than raw AI output. Every user interaction is logged, allowing the system to detect knowledge gaps and generate follow-up content automatically. This makes Cognita more than just a content delivery tool as it actively adapts to the learner.

sections.heading: What we learned ✏️
sections.text: Building an adaptive system requires strong coordination between retrieval models, state tracking, and user analytics. We learned how to design schemas that can store lesson metadata, interaction logs, and progress in a consistent way. Prompt engineering was critical to ensure the AI generated structured, assessable lessons. The hardest part was creating a real-time state management system that tied frontend interactions back into the backend analytics, which in turn informed future lessons.

sections.heading: What’s next for Cognita 👣
sections.text: We plan to extend support beyond PDFs to include PowerPoints, videos, and web pages, making it easier for companies to reuse all their training resources. Integrations with HR systems like Workday and BambooHR will help embed Cognita into existing workflows. Multi-language support is also on our roadmap to help global companies onboard interns in their native languages. In the long term, we want to add features like customizable certification systems and automated quiz generation for compliance and ongoing training.
